newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - BONN DESPERATELY SEEKS TO PLUG BUDGET GAPS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BONN DESPERATELY SEEKS TO PLUG BUDGET GAPS.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl is desperately seeking 50 billion marks to fill budget gaps for 1997 and 1998, allowing Germany to qualify for the single European currency, sources in his coalition said on Tuesday.
But as Kohl battles to cut the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), it will inevitably be higher than the government's forecast, they said.
The government had hoped a revaluation of the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves would help to plug the gap.

But coalition sources said the profits would be transferred to Bonn only in 1998, the year after countries have to meet targets for economic and monetary union (EMU) laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.
For 1997 alone, tax revenues are about 9.1 billion marks short of budget targets, while outlays for unemployment benefits are about 20 billion marks higher than budgeted.
Lower interest rates and a spending freeze will help to trim outlays, and the government plans to sell land and other assets, budget experts in the centre-right coalition told Reuters.
The sale of more state-owned shares in Deutsche Telekom should bring another 10 billion to 15 billion marks.
Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats, who strongly oppose tax increases, have floated the idea of simply allowing the deficit to swell.

But that would require a supplementary budget, and it would present a potential constitutional conflict. Germany's constitution forbids the federal government from allowing its deficit to exceed its investment spending.
The forecast deficit of 53.3 billion marks is already nearly equal to the 59 billion marks in 1997 government investment.
A higher deficit would be allowed only if the government declared a "disturbance of economic equilibrium".
For 1998, tax revenues are now seen 14 billion marks lower than previous projections, and higher unemployment revenues could widen the budget gap to 30 billion marks.
Again, the coalition is staking its fate on the sale of Telekom shares as a revenue source.

But privatisation revenues will not be enough. Cuts in social spending are being considered, but will be difficult to implement because of Social Democrat opposition in an election year, the coalition sources said.
While the FDP is opposed to tax increases, Kohl's Christian Democrats see no alternative. A one pfennig rise in petroleum tax would bring in about 800 million marks.
The government has left itself about 18 billion marks in leeway above the planned budget deficit levels before it would exceed the target of three percent of GDP laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.
Increases in pension reserves could boost this leeway even higher. But privatisation revenues cannot be counted toward relieving the deficit.
That is where the Buba's gold reserves come into play. A revaluation of the gold closer to market levels could bring Bonn seven to 10 billion marks this year, nearly 0.3 percent of GDP.

Without the revaluation, Germany's budget deficit is almost certain to be 3.1 to 3.3 percent of GDP, a possibility that Finance Minister Theo Waigel rejects even though opposition parties and private sector banks have said they could tolerate a slight exceeding of the Maastricht target.
But Kohl's coalition backed down earlier on Tuesday on the controversial revaulation plan after parliamentary deputies from Kohl's party sharply criticised the proposal.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
